Balanced and Disk Trees

A search tree is only fast when it is short. Watch sorted keys ruin a plain tree, AVL rotations and red black colours keep a tree short, B trees split their way to perfect balance, and a B+ tree scan a range the way a database does.

Part 1

⚖️Why balance matters

The Trees chapter showed that a binary search tree is only fast when it is short. Insert keys that are already sorted and every new key becomes a right child. The tree turns into a chain, and a search walks every node. A self balancing tree does a little extra work after each insert so that its height stays close to log₂ n, whatever order the keys arrive in.

best possible height = ⌈log₂(n + 1)⌉    1000 keys → 10 levels
Search, insert and delete all cost O(height). Keeping the height at O(log n) is the whole point of every tree in this chapter.
Part 2

🔄Rotations and AVL trees

An AVL tree stores the height of every node. The balance factor is the left height minus the right height, and it must stay at −1, 0 or +1. After an insert, walk back up. The first node that reaches ±2 is fixed with a rotation, which lifts one child up and moves the parent down, while keeping every key in search order.

CaseThe new key wentFix
LLleft, then leftrotate right at the unbalanced node
RRright, then rightrotate left at the unbalanced node
LRleft, then rightrotate left at the child, then right at the node
RLright, then leftrotate right at the child, then left at the node
An AVL tree with n keys is never taller than about 1.44 log₂ n. One insert needs at most one single or one double rotation.
Part 3

🔴Red black trees, the left leaning way

A red black tree colours each node red or black and keeps two rules. No red node has a red child, and every path from the root down to an empty spot passes the same number of black nodes. Together they keep the longest path at most twice the shortest, so the height is at most 2 log₂(n + 1).

The left leaning version, described by Robert Sedgewick in 2008, adds one more rule: a red link always leans left. Then an insert needs only three small fixes, checked on the way back up.

You seeFix
a red right child and a black left childrotate left
a red left child whose left child is red toorotate right
both children redflip colours: children turn black, the node turns red
Java's TreeMap and TreeSet are red black trees. Red black trees rotate less often than AVL trees when keys change a lot, which is why libraries tend to pick them.
Part 4

🧱B trees: many keys per node

A B tree lets one node hold many sorted keys and have one more child than it has keys. With minimum degree t, every node except the root holds between t − 1 and 2t − 1 keys. Here t = 2, so each node holds 1 to 3 keys. When a node on the way down is full, it splits: the middle key moves up into the parent. The tree only grows taller when the root splits, so every leaf stays on the same level.

keys per node: t − 1 … 2t − 1    children per node: t … 2t
A B tree with t = 2 is also called a 2-3-4 tree. A left leaning red black tree is a binary way of drawing a 2-3 tree, where a red link glues two keys into one node.
Part 5

💾B+ trees, disks and databases

Reading from a disk is slow compared with memory, so the number of nodes read matters more than the work inside a node. A B tree node is sized to fill one disk page, so a node can have hundreds of children and the tree stays only a few levels tall.

Databases mostly use the B+ tree variant. Internal nodes hold only signposts that guide the search. Every real key and record sits in a leaf, and the leaves are linked in order. A range query walks down once, then slides along the leaves without climbing back up.

MySQL's InnoDB, PostgreSQL and SQLite all keep their indexes in B tree variants. File systems such as Btrfs, XFS and NTFS use them to find files and blocks.
Part 6

🗂️Ordered maps in each language

You rarely write a balanced tree yourself. You use the ordered map or set your language provides, and ask it questions a hash map cannot answer: the smallest key, the biggest key, the floor (biggest key at most x), the ceiling (smallest key at least x), and every key in a range.

LanguageWhat to useInsert
JavaTreeMap, TreeSet: floorKey, ceilingKey, subMapO(log n)
Pythona sorted list with bisect, or the third party sortedcontainersO(n) shift for a plain list
JavaScript, TypeScripta sorted array with your own binary searchO(n) shift
A sorted list answers floor and ceiling in O(log n), but each insert shifts items. That is fine for thousands of keys and slow for millions of changing keys, where a real balanced tree wins.
